title: Caravaggio and Chiaroscuro
subject: art
description: **Michelangelo Merisi**, known as Caravaggio, changed painting forever with brutal realism and an extreme contrast of light and shadow: chiaroscuro.

hero.hook: Saints with dirty feet, lit like a stage: art would never be the same.

blocks.text: **Michelangelo Merisi**, known as **Caravaggio** (1571-1610), broke the rules of ideal beauty inherited from the Renaissance. He set the sacred next to daily life: beggars, taverns, tired bodies.

His weapon was radical chiaroscuro. Bodies leap out of the darkness as if caught in a spotlight. That break announced the spirit of [[Baroque painting]] and turned the viewer into the witness of a drama.

blocks.caption: Caravaggio, a painter of genius and a figure of turbulent Roman life

blocks.text: Born near Milan, Caravaggio reached Rome around **1593**. His breakthrough came in **1600** with the canvases of the Contarelli Chapel, in the church of San Luigi dei Francesi. *The Calling of Saint Matthew* stunned Rome: here the sacred had the face of the street.
In Malta, he was made a knight of the Order, then jailed for attacking a superior officer. He escaped from a fort thought to be impregnable, using a hemp rope.

His life was as violent as his paintings. In **1606**, in a street brawl, he killed **Ranuccio Tomassoni**. Sentenced to death, he fled to Naples, then Malta, then Sicily. Hunted and wounded, he died at **38** in [[Porto Ercole]], a few days before a papal pardon.

Caravaggio invented **tenebrism**, an extreme form of chiaroscuro. No more soft light stroking the shapes: instead an opaque darkness, and bodies that burst out of it with sculptural force. The light is artificial, like a spotlight on a stage.

blocks.caption: In tenebrism, black focuses the eye on the drama

blocks.text: To get that lighting, he worked in a studio with black walls and a single small skylight set high up.

By cutting out settings and landscapes, he forces attention onto faces and gestures. This light also served the [[Counter-Reformation]]: the Catholic Church wanted to move the faithful. In his hands, light becomes the grace that strikes the soul without warning.

sections.title: Saints who look like the street

blocks.text: What shocked people most was his refusal to idealize. He picked his models off the street: workers, beggars, courtesans. The Virgin and the apostles have wrinkles, dirty feet, tired bodies.

blocks.caption: Madonna of the Pilgrims: bare, dirty feet in the foreground

blocks.text: *The Death of the Virgin* was rejected: rumor said he had used a drowned woman as his model. *Madonna of the Pilgrims* shocked viewers with the dirty feet of the kneeling poor. He refused the artifice of [[Mannerism]], the graceful, distorted style that came before him. For him, salvation was aimed first at the humble.
His first version of *Saint Matthew and the Angel* showed an evangelist with dirty feet who looked unschooled. The patrons demanded that he paint it again.

sections.title: Caravaggism: a Europe under his influence

blocks.text: He founded no school, yet his style spread anyway: **Caravaggism**. [[Artemisia Gentileschi]] in Italy, Georges de La Tour in France, Zurbarán in Spain, Rubens in Flanders. Later, **Rembrandt** would inherit his poetry of shadow, and **Velázquez** his sense of the dignity of ordinary people.

blocks.text: Forgotten for two centuries, he was rediscovered in the 20th century. His tight framing and his light still shape film and photography.
Caravaggio (1571-1610) imposed tenebrism and a radical social realism. By painting the sacred with models found on the street, he became the spiritual father of Baroque painting.
